name: Mapudungun
region: Wallmapu: Araucanía, Biobío, Los Ríos and Los Lagos in Chile, Santiago, and Neuquén, Río Negro and Chubut in Argentina
summary: The language of the Mapuche people, «the speech of the land». Its verb strings suffixes together and has three numbers: one, two and many.

conjugator.label: Verb
conjugator.hint: Type the verb in the 1st person, as the grammar names it: txipan «go out», küzawün «work», amun «go», zugun «speak». You can also type just the root (txipa, küzaw).

own.hint: Type any verb in the 1st person (ending in -n or -ün) and its meaning in English. The suffixes are the same for every verb.
own.label: Verb

source.short: Hernández, Ramos and Huenchulaf, Gramática básica de la lengua mapuche (2006)
source.full: Arturo Hernández Sallés, Nelly Ramos Pizarro and Rosa Huenchulaf Cayuqueo, Gramática básica de la lengua mapuche, vol. 1 (Temuco: Universidad Católica de Temuco / CONADI, 2006), §7, for the verb and the Azümchefe alphabet; Elba Jara Trecanahuel, Gilberto Melipil Melipil and Juan Ñancupil Railaf, Cuaderno pedagógico de mapudügun (Servicio Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural, Maule region, 2020), for the present with -le / -küle and the vocabulary; Ineke Smeets, A Grammar of Mapuche (Mouton de Gruyter, 2008), for the 1st person plural -(iy)iñ.

about: Mapudungun, or Mapuzugun, is the language of the Mapuche people. It is spoken in Wallmapu, the Mapuche land on both sides of the Andes: in south-central Chile, above all in Araucanía, and in Argentine Patagonia, and also in Santiago, where many families moved. It has some one to two hundred thousand speakers, nearly all bilingual.

It is an isolate: it has no known relatives beyond its own varieties, such as Huilliche in the south or Pehuenche in the mountains. Its verb is agglutinative: suffixes are added to the root in a fixed order, ten or more in a single word, to say who, to whom, when, where and how.

It has no single spelling: the Unified Alphabet, Raguileo and Azümchefe, adopted by CONADI and Chile's Ministry of Education, live side by side. Today it is taught in intercultural schools and in community workshops working to revitalize it.

orthography.intro: We use the Azümchefe alphabet, the one in Hernández, Ramos and Huenchulaf's grammar and the one adopted by the Chilean state; its name is made of its first letters (a, z, ü, m, ch, e, f, i) and means «the one who teaches». Each sound has its letter, and h marks the sounds made with the tongue between the teeth.
notes: ü is a u with spread, unrounded lips: karü «green». Unstressed it sounds like a dull e.
r is said with the tip of the tongue curled back, like an English r but softer: relmu «rainbow». tx is a dragged tr, as in Chilean Spanish: txomü «cloud».
g is the ng of sing, never a Spanish g: ge «eye». The soft Spanish g sound is written q: reqle «seven».
nh, lh and t with the tongue between the teeth are kept apart from n, l and t: nhamunh «foot». Also, sh and t' mark affectionate or scornful speech: ufisha «sheep», wezat'e «villain».

Other spellings write the same sounds differently: the Unified Alphabet uses d, tr, ng and ñ (mapudungun, trewa «dog»), and Raguileo uses c, x, g and v. That is why the language appears as mapudungun, mapuzugun or mapudüngun.

grammar.intro: A Mapuche verb is a root followed by suffixes in a fixed order: those that change the meaning, negation, tense and last mood, person and number. A verb is named by its 1st person indicative: txipan «I went out», küzawün «I worked».

items.description: -la in the indicative, -no in the hypothetical, -kil in the imperative.

blocks.title: Three numbers
blocks.description: The 1st and 2nd persons always tell singular, dual (two people) and plural (three or more) apart. In the 3rd person the dual and plural (-gu, -gün) are optional: küla zomo txipay «three women went out».

blocks.title: No present tense
blocks.description: The basic form doesn't mark tense: with action verbs it reads as past, with state verbs as present. For what is happening now, -le is used, or -küle after a consonant.

blocks.title: Every affix of the verb
blocks.description: Every piece a verb can take, in the order it goes: root, suffixes that change the verb, aspect, negation, tense, object and, last, mood and person. They can be combined: amu-pa-ke-n «I always come».

items.translation: I looked for it for him

items.meaning: not (in the hypothetical and non-finite forms)
a past that no longer holds, or a failed attempt

items.translation: I went, you went, he went

items.meaning: indicative dual: we two, you two, they two
indicative plural: we, you all, they
imperative: you, you two, you all
participle: the one who does; when
items.translation: the one who went, when he went

blocks.title: Who to whom
blocks.description: The verb also carries the other person. The higher person leads (1st › 2nd › 3rd), whether it acts or receives: zuguen is «I was spoken to by you».

tenses.name: Indicative
tenses.description: The basic form, with no tense: past for action verbs (txipan «I went out»), present for state verbs (nien «I have»).

tenses.name: Progressive
tenses.description: What is happening now: -le, or -küle after a consonant.

tenses.name: Habitual
tenses.description: What one always or usually does (-ke).

tenses.name: Perfective
tenses.description: What was over before a given moment (-wye, -üwye).

tenses.name: -fu past
tenses.description: What was and no longer is, or was tried in vain: amufun «I had gone (but…)», niefun «I had».

tenses.name: Conditional
tenses.description: What would happen, what is possible and what is polite (-afu): ¿konafuyiñ? «may we come in?».

tenses.name: Hypothetical
tenses.description: The mood of conditions and suppositions (-l, -ül): if it happens.

tenses.name: Imperative
tenses.description: Orders to you, you two or you all (-ge, -mu, -mün).

tenses.name: Let's
tenses.description: Inviting others to do something together, with the indicative forms (-yu, -yiñ).

tenses.name: Let him do it
tenses.description: Let me do it (-chi) and let him or them do it (-pe, -pegu, -pegün).

lexicon.note: A weather verb, used in the 3rd person: mawüni «it rained», mawünküley «it is raining»; with -ma, mawünman «it rained on me».
